report.title: Evidence room
report.subtitle: You confirmed a change, but one survey cannot prove the cause.
report.photoEvidence: Earlier and current views can be compared
report.doEvidence: The survey unit saved a water-and-habitat clue
report.foodWebHint: Arrows show possible feeding links. A missing node is not proof of extinction.
report.puzzleHint: Each piece reflects this survey only: photographed, observed, or not observed here.
report.foodWebDragHint: Drag the 4 fish cards into their roles to complete this food chain.
report.foodWebWrongZone: That role does not fit this organism. Try another zone.
report.foodLessonTitle: First, learn how to read a food chain
report.foodLessonDefinition: A food chain shows who eats whom. Energy moves from food to the organism that eats it, so arrows point from prey to eater.
report.foodLessonExample: Seagrass  →  Small fish  →  Large reef fish
report.foodLessonWeb: Correct! A food chain shows feeding relationships among organisms. Now use today's fish to complete one food chain.
report.notCause: The observations do not prove one cause
report.singleReading: One reading cannot represent every time, place, or depth
report.nextStep: A longer, distributed monitoring plan is needed
report.callout:
A changed image is evidence, not a cause.
We still need to find what changed in the water.
report.note: Next: follow the breathing clue and decide what must be measured over time.
report.recapStart: Finish the food chain, then take the quick recap
report.recap.q1: Can one afternoon DO reading tell us whether low oxygen occurred before dawn?
report.recap.q1b: No, we need measurements over time
report.recap.q2: If surface DO is normal, must near-bed DO also be normal?
report.recap.q2a: Yes, all depths are the same
report.recap.q3: There are fewer marine organisms today. Does that prove low oxygen is the only cause?
report.recap.q3a:
No; the photo shows fewer organisms,
but cannot prove low oxygen is the only cause
report.recap.q3b: Yes; fewer organisms can only mean low oxygen
report.recap.q4: If small fish decline sharply, what might happen to other organisms in the food chain?
report.recap.q4a: Larger reef fish and other organisms that depend on them may also decline
report.recap.q4b: Only the small fish change; all other organisms stay the same
report.recapFoodWebOutcome: Correct! A food chain shows how organisms depend on one another. Low DO may affect small fish and then larger reef fish, but we still need continuous DO data across locations and depths to test that connection.
report.recapCorrect: Correct! That is the monitoring problem for the next chapter.
report.doBridgeDefinition: Dissolved oxygen is oxygen in water that fish and other organisms breathe, abbreviated DO.
report.doBridgeWater: Oxygen in water: for fish and other aquatic life
report.doBridgeLow: Low DO: aquatic life may lack oxygen
report.doBridgeProblem: PROBLEM — A photo shows one moment, and one reading may miss low oxygen near the seabed before dawn.
report.doBridgeSolution: THEREFORE — Monitor continuously at multiple locations and depths.
report.doBridgeListenFirst: Listen to the full narration first

opening.photoInspectHint: Drag or zoom when needed. Use the arrows to change photos.
opening.photoHotspotHint: MISSION: select the yellow ring to find an old ocean clue.
opening.photoHotspotDefault: Select the yellow ring in the photograph.
opening.hotspot.s1.fish.reaction: Wow—there used to be many Chinese damselfish here, in more than one group.
opening.hotspot.s1.fish.record: Several mid-water groups are visible. Abundance should only be compared against the same framing and station.
opening.hotspot.s1.station.reaction: This cable and instrument are our landmark for returning to the same view.
opening.hotspot.s1.station.record: A fixed instrument provides a spatial reference and reduces framing differences during repeat photography.
opening.hotspot.s1.habitat.reaction: The seabed is not just a background—the fish are using this habitat.
opening.hotspot.s1.habitat.record: Seagrass, reef pieces and bottom structure provide shelter and feeding space, and are evidence worth comparing.
opening.hotspot.s2.raft.reaction: The second station really is beside the fish raft—the net-cage structure is unmistakable.
opening.hotspot.s2.raft.record: The raft and net cage define this station. Today's framing should retain the same structure as a location reference.
opening.hotspot.s2.fish.reaction: The fish are not lined up; some are hidden around the cage.
opening.hotspot.s2.fish.record: Visible abundance changes with occlusion, light and movement, so repeat observations matter more than one frame.
opening.hotspot.s2.station.reaction: This monitor sits close to the raft, where water conditions may change quickly.
opening.hotspot.s2.station.record: A station near aquaculture needs repeated measurements to separate tides, operations and possible low-oxygen events.
opening.hotspot.s3.seabed.reaction: The inner-bay clue is really on the bottom, where sea cucumbers and other benthic life belong.
opening.hotspot.s3.seabed.record: Benthic organisms and bottom structure suit fixed-point comparison. Sea cucumbers should stay in contact with the seabed.
opening.hotspot.s3.station.reaction: The instrument reaches the seabed, and this third station is shallower than the others.
opening.hotspot.s3.station.record: Measurements from different depths cannot be merged blindly; instrument height and seabed position both matter.
opening.hotspot.s3.fish.reaction: There are not many fish in this photo, which reminds me to read the whole habitat.
opening.hotspot.s3.fish.record: Few fish in one frame does not mean a population vanished. Trend claims need repeated views at the same place and time.
opening.hotspot.s1.summary.reaction: Wow—the bay entrance used to show more than one fish group, with the cable and seabed clearly visible too.
opening.hotspot.s1.summary.record: Match the fixed instrument, fish groups and seabed habitat before comparing relative abundance.
opening.hotspot.s2.summary.reaction: This station is beside the fish raft; the cage, fish and instrument all help us recover the same viewpoint.
opening.hotspot.s2.summary.record: Fish may hide behind the cage or leave the frame, so keep the raft as a landmark and repeat the observation over time.
opening.hotspot.s3.summary.reaction: The inner-bay clue is on the seabed: sea cucumbers, benthic life and instrument position matter more than a distant fish.
opening.hotspot.s3.summary.record: Benthic life stays on the seabed and depth must be recorded. Few fish in one frame does not prove a population vanished.

lab.scienceNote: DO is oxygen in seawater that organisms can breathe. Teaching simulation: oxygen changes the sensing film's optical signal, then the reader converts that change into DO. Real materials, calibration and performance require final technical data.

lab.consoleTitle: Challenge: use a monitoring network to find a hidden low-oxygen event
lab.consoleBody: Success needs all 9 points covered, complete data at all 9 points, and a total cost no higher than $3600.
lab.compareTitle: Which method can find low oxygen at dawn?
lab.compareBody: Learn the three recording methods, then decide how to deploy them. The result appears after your 24-hour run.
lab.compareManualMethodBody: One vessel visit samples surface, mid-water and near-bed at one location, but each depth gets only one moment.
lab.compareManualMethodTag: 3 DEPTHS AT ONE SITE · ONE MOMENT
lab.compareFixedMethodBody: Each conventional probe monitors one point. In this simulation biofouling breaks its link and a repair uses more budget.
lab.compareFixedMethodTag: ONE POINT · SIGNAL BREAK · REPAIR COST
lab.compareSensorMethodBody:
Continuous multi-point monitoring
UV helps suppress biofouling
Replaceable sensing film
lab.compareSensorMethodTag: MANY PLACES · MANY DEPTHS · CONTINUOUS TIME
lab.compareManualNarration:
THREE DEPTHS AT ONE SITE,

lab.compareFixedNarration:

lab.compareSensorNarration:

lab.summaryTitle: What did we learn from this investigation?
lab.summaryBody: Take away the three most important discoveries.
lab.summaryOceanBody: Fish use gills to take in DO from water. Food chains connect, so a change in one organism may affect others.
lab.summaryEvidenceBody: One photo or reading is only one moment. Compare times, places and depths so important changes are not missed.
lab.summarySensorBody: Oxygen changes the film's optical signal. UV helps suppress growth and replaceable film supports longer monitoring; this does not mean fouling is impossible.
lab.summaryMethodCompare: The same 24 hours: what did each tool record?
lab.summaryCompare: Compare old and new photos from the same place and a similar angle; describe visible change first.
lab.summaryFoodWeb: A food chain shows interdependence; a change in one organism may affect others.
lab.summaryGills: Fish take oxygen from water with gills; scales are not breathing organs.
lab.summaryDo: Dissolved Oxygen (DO) is oxygen in water that aquatic organisms can use.
lab.summaryLimits: One photo or reading represents one moment and cannot prove a cause by itself.
lab.summaryNetwork: Reliable monitoring needs multiple sites, multiple depths and continuous measurements.
lab.summaryFilm: Oxygen changes the film's optical signal; a reader turns the change into saved data.
lab.summaryListenFirst: Listen to the full learning summary first
lab.finalQuizTitle: Take away the investigation's key ideas
lab.finalQuizBody: Connect the observation, breathing clue and monitoring method from this mission.
lab.finalQuizQuestion: Which method best checks for low oxygen near the seabed before dawn?
lab.finalQuizA: Measure surface water once in the afternoon
lab.finalQuizB: Record continuously near the seabed and compare several locations
lab.finalQuizCorrect: Correct! Continuous time, near-bed depth and multiple locations fill the gaps in a one-off survey.
lab.finalQuizTryAgain: Think again: what time and depth would one afternoon surface reading miss?
lab.finalQuizSensorQuestion: What is an advantage of the next-generation dissolved oxygen sensor?
lab.finalQuizSensorA:
It can form a continuous multi-point network,
suppress fouling with UV, and use replaceable film
lab.finalQuizSensorB: It only measures once when a vessel arrives and can record only the surface
lab.finalQuizSensorCorrect: Correct! Multiple points, depths and continuous time make dawn low oxygen harder to miss.
lab.finalQuizSensorTryAgain: Think again: the next-generation dissolved oxygen sensor is designed to fill gaps left by one-off samples and broken links.
lab.endingBody: You found change in old photographs, then completed the evidence with monitoring across locations, depths and time.
lab.endingRealScience: Oceanographers and scientists really use sensors, vessels and long-term records to care for the ocean. Every reliable observation helps us understand and protect marine ecosystems.
lab.endingProtect: Carry your curiosity with you—and help notice and protect our ocean.

opening.guide.s1.title: Chinese damselfish
opening.guide.s1.body: A small reef fish with a blue-grey body and a distinct yellow-orange caudal peduncle and tail. Old photos show several together.
opening.guide.s2.title: Hong Kong grouper
opening.guide.s2.body: A marine reef fish that shelters near structures and ambushes smaller animals.
opening.guide.s3.title: Sea cucumber
opening.guide.s3.body: A slow-moving benthic animal that lives on the seabed. Record it together with the surrounding bottom habitat.
